permitted_claims.statement: The earliest writing implies trained specialists, but their identities, recruitment and institutional status are poorly recoverable.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Lists and handwriting variation provide indirect evidence, not biographies.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: The best archaeological evidence for formal curricula comes from later household and institutional contexts, especially the Old Babylonian period.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Later evidence cannot be projected unchanged onto Uruk.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: Edubba was not necessarily a single standardized temple-run school system across Mesopotamian history.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Literary school texts use institutional language, but excavated teaching often occurs in houses.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: Scribal competence included copying, calculation, lexical knowledge and genre conventions, not merely decoding signs.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Curriculum differed by period, place and career path.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: Access was restricted and socially consequential, but no reliable percentage for literacy or a universal male-only rule can be derived.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Named female scribes and elite women exist in some periods; corpus is not population-representative.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: House F at Old Babylonian Nippur provides an unusually contextualized household training sequence, not proof of a universal Mesopotamian school system.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Its more than 1,400 tablets make the sequence unusually rich but also locally exceptional.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use House F as an illustrative, high-resolution anchor explicitly labeled non-representative of all periods.

permitted_claims.statement: Professional title, functional competence and broad literacy must be mapped separately; some later archives show on-the-job or non-professional use outside a single formal school track.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Survival still favors administrative settings and trained writers.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Describe capabilities and work roles instead of assigning a modern literate/illiterate binary.

permitted_claims.statement: Named women and female-authored or female-voiced texts demonstrate access in some settings but cannot establish population rates or unmediated authorship.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Scribal mediation, elite selection and uneven survival complicate attribution.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use specific women only with period, role, mediation and representativeness labels.

permitted_claims.statement: Lexical lists form a continuous knowledge-organizing tradition from the earliest writing through later cuneiform cultures.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Continuity involved copying, reordering and transformation, not static preservation.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use only with the stated confidence and boundary.

permitted_claims.statement: ETCSL's 394 literary compositions are modern composites based on late-third- and early-second-millennium manuscripts, so they are evidence for textual tradition rather than transparent transcripts of an original speaker.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Individual manuscripts can preserve locally and chronologically specific variants when cited at tablet level.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Attribute translation and edition; identify composite status and avoid invented authorial interiority.

permitted_claims.statement: P228744 is a fragmented Old Babylonian lexical school tablet excavated at Nippur and a witness to the OB Nippur Ura 03 composite Q000001.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: The obverse is missing and the record does not preserve detailed stratigraphy; formal school material cannot establish population-wide literacy.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use as a representative case of formal lexical classification and copying within the Nippur training tradition only.

permitted_claims.statement: ETCSL 3.1.19 is a modern composite of the Puzur-Shulgi royal letter tradition assembled from multiple Old Babylonian manuscripts, not a contemporary Ur III dispatch.
permitted_claims.counterevidence: Individual witnesses such as 3N-T311/IM 58418 preserve substantial portions and can be cited separately, but no one witness equals the complete ETCSL text.
permitted_claims.narrative_implication: Use to show retrospective political/literary memory and scribal copying; always distinguish narrated event, manuscript date and modern reconstruction.
